questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I visited Canada a couple of years back and fell head over heels in love with the country - The nature, the people, the multiculturalism - It simply had everything I could possibly want. Furthermore, I had been told that specifically British Columbia (BC), a province, in Canada was a really stunning place, so I searched for universities in BC. I knew that I also wanted to go to a place that could contribute academically to my studies, and therefore the choice fell naturally to the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Vancouver. UBC has an excellent reputation both academically, socially, and culturally. It is almost twice the size of KU and has an enormous percentage of international students, so I knew that it would be possible to connect with people from all over the world, which was a big wish for me. UBC is also a giant campus, which means that you can really get that "famous" campus experience, where you study and live on campus, which was a fantastic experience for me. It really is just like you see in the movies ;)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My overall experience was absolutely incredible! The only reason that it only gets an 8/10 is due to the infamous, annoying COVID, which affected my experience both before and a bit during my stay. Before going, COVID added a lot of problems and insecurities to the planning, and during the first month of my stay, everything was still online. We were also required to wear face masks during the entire stay there etc. But that is really the only bad thing I have to say about my experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy - UBC has a really helpful team at their exchange office Go Global, who are always ready to help you with whatever you need, whether it is about academic questions, housing, or any other issues you may encounter.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't really receive any assistance because I didn't need it  - But UBC had made sure that I knew exactly where to seek help if it had been needed. My roommates at my dorm also helped me a lot with learning to find my way around campus, helpful tips, etc., so I got all the support I needed there :)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Before arrival, the Go Global team held several orientation sessions, so I think we were all very prepared when we actually arrived at UBC. Furthermore, when I moved into my housing, I also got a lot of information from them, and then my roommates helped me with the rest - So really, I have no complaints.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are several options available for on-campus housing. You fill out a housing application where you can then prioritize if you for instance would rather live in a shared apartment, dorm housing, or studio apartment. None of the options at UBC are cheap - It is a rather expensive place to live. Typically as exchange students, there are three different places they put students. Walter Gage, which primarily consists of apartments that you share with 5 other people (that is where I lived), Saltwater residence, which is studio apartments, or Fairview, which are these townhouse-style houses that you share with around 4 other people (as I remember it). My room at Walter Gage cost about 4800 kr. a month, so very similar to Copenhagen prices. Everything else was more expensive

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: All the typical exchange housing options have cooking facilities, but it is also possible to purchase different types of meal plans. There were both UBC eats, which is a type of Hellofresh concept, or you could buy these types of plans where you got a discount at all the eating places on campus (which there are plenty of, UBC is giant). I did not purchase any of these, since it was cheaper to just cook on my own.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
First of all, UBC housing is expensive, especially if you like me are used to a cheap dorm room here in Denmark. I even got the cheapest one at UBC with my room at Walter Gage, but I know other people who for instance got a studio apartment, which I think was about 7000 kr a month. So calculate to spend a lot of money on housing. Furthermore, only about 50 % actually get on-campus housing, so you might wanna be prepared to find something off-campus. Also, you only get one offer from UBC - So even though you make a prioritized list, you are not guaranteed to get anything from your top 3, and if you want to live on-campus, you just have to say yes to whatever they offer. I do really recommend living on campus since it is such a unique experience that we don't really get in Denmark. UBC is like its own little city (it has the size for it), so to be a part of that really completed my exchange experience. 
One more thing to be aware of is that people in Canada start university when they are pretty young, so be prepared to live with people who are only 18-19 years old and who are completely new to living away from home. I had some lovely roommates, but I know that others encountered problems with roommates who were very immature.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a nice room at Walter Gage, but it was pretty worn down. The kitchen facilities worked, but that was also about it - Don't expect fancy indoor facilities at a place like the Gage.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration process was pretty easy - If you just follow UBC's instructions, the process should be smooth.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
As I remember it, there were two steps to it. 
First, you had to send UBC a list with 10 courses that you were thinking of taking while at UBC - It is basically just to make sure that you have had some thoughts about it. You don't have to actually take any of those. Later in the process, you had to send them a list of courses you actually wanted, and then the Go Global office actually did the registration for you. Then sometime later before your stay you could log in to the UBC portal and see which courses you had been registered for - I had gotten registered for 4 courses, which is the amount I wanted. Some of the ones I had wanted were full, but then they had just registered me for some of the other ones that I listed, so it worked out fine :)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always write to the Go Global office, and you were also welcome to write to the professors if you had any academic questions about course content, exams, etc. They always replied really quickly and were very nice. The only problems I experienced were back at KU with the KU offices, but never with UBC.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the amount and the courses that I had listed as wanted options :)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to contact your professors about the courses - Sometimes the information about the course is not very specific on the UBC website, so it can be really helpful to get a better explanation from the profs themselves.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall I was satisfied with the academic program, although I do have some critical remarks that I elaborate on further down.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I experienced the academic level of the courses at UBC to be lower than at KU. I'm used to doing a lot of work at KU in classes with relatively big papers to write all the time, and there is an expectation that you are capable of analyzing, discussing, and critically reflecting on complicated theories, methods, etc. At UBC, you were basically just expected to memorize everything that was said during lectures and in your textbook.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching only took place as lectures - There was no classroom-style teaching at all in the courses I took, although the professors were very open to questions so that sometimes helped facilitate a bit of discussion in the lectures. You did not have to actively participate in lectures, but if you wanted a good grade, it was definitely necessary to take thorough notes since a lot of the exam questions were based on solely lecture material.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I took the following courses: 
- PSYC 102: Introduction to Social Psychology, Personality Psychology, Developmental Psychology, and Clinical Psychology
- PSYC 300a: Abnormal Psychology
- PSYC 314: Health Psychology
- PSYC 350a: Psychological aspects of human sexuality

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend PSYC 314 and PSYC 350a. Both courses are not really something you can take at KU, and they were both extremely interesting and taught by some very talented researchers, Dr. King, and Dr. Goldsmith. 
- Health psychology changed a lot about my way of thinking about the connection between the mind, brain, and body, and has opened my eyes to an entirely new field in psychology. 
- Psychological aspects of human sexuality can be seen as an extremely elaborate form of sexual education from a psychological point of view. I have learned a lot from that course that I did not know - It treats sexuality as a very broad term, so expect to learn everything from the development of fetuses to critical discussions of gender to the male anatomy. Everything having to do with sex, sexuality etc is covered in that course.

Housing DKK per month *

Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *

Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I was surprised at how expensive phone plans are in Canada - Definitely calculate into your budget to spend at least 300 kr a month on it - And that is probably only if you can get a good deal. Besides that, be prepared for the fact that you might need to buy a lot of kitchen equipment. I was lucky enough to have roommates that were willing to share their plates, pots and pans etc, but I know a lot of people who had to buy all that stuff, which quickly adds up to a lot.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
More expensive: Phone plans and groceries - Canada, especially Vancouver, is not a cheap place to live. Specifically fruit, vegetables, and meat were really expensive, so calculate that into your budget
I don't think that there was anything that was less expensive - Again, Vancouver is not a cheap place to live.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Due to COVID, a lot of the usual welcoming events and such were unfortunately canceled, so it was very much up to ourselves to get to know other people. But since all exchange students are really desperate to make friends, there were quickly formed several groups on Facebook, WhatsApp, etc, where meet-ups, happenings, trips, and such were planned.
Besides that, UBC also has a huge variety of different clubs and such that you can become a part of - I did not since I was only there for 1 term, but if I had been there longer I definitely would have signed up for some of those, since that is also an excellent way to meet other people. 
UBC has a very rich campus life where there is always tons of stuff happening - UBC for instance has several bars, its own nightclub, and such, so there is always lots to do on campus.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are plenty of activities to do - See my comment above. Besides that, UBC for instance has several gyms where membership is really cheap, so you can stay in shape while eating all those Tim Hortons donuts. The activities I participated in were primarily arranged by exchange students (including myself), so we really made it work on our own.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend checking out the sports events - UBC is very proud of their Thunderbird teams, and has teams in Hockey, baseball, basketball, volley, and many other types of sports. Going to watch those games are always fun! Here you can really get that famous North American University movie vibe! 
Besides that I would definitely just go into everything with a yes-mentality - Of course not so much that you end up getting stressed out, but go out and meet people, go to the events, and get the maximum out of your stay!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Vancouver is famous for easy access to skiing, hiking, watersports, etc - You can seriously ski in the morning, and jump into the water in the afternoon! So this place is perfect for all outdoor lovers, no matter what you enjoy! Personally, I love hiking, so all my weekends were spent in the mountains. Other than that, Vancouver Island is also a must-do - It's the most amazing nature place, the island is the size of Jutland, so there is plenty to do! I ended my stay with an American westcoast adventure because Vancouver is also so close to the border. So definitely calculate on spending a lot of money on trips  - There are so many beautiful places to visit, both in British Columbia, bot also in some of the nearby provinces, for instance Alberta that is home to the famous Banff and Jasper nationalpark, which i would definitely recommend seeing!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Canada is in many ways similar to Denmark, except just nicer. They are very open to everyone, so expect to have a lot of conversations with random strangers ;) Canada really lives up to all the stereotypes that everyone is nice - But remember, that when people ask you “How are you?”, they don't necessarily want to hear everything about your day ;)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just be open and friendly, then everything will be just fine! And if you don't know what else to say, just start talking about hockey.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't really find anything particularly challenging - Maybe just that Canada took COVID a lot more seriously than Denmark did at that time, so I found that my opinions about COVID policies were way more relaxed than a lot of the people i met i Canada.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and friendliness - Denmark could really learn something from Canada about welcoming foreigners, and just in general taking more notice of the people you meet in your everyday life.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. In the beginning it can be hard to find a balance between your FOMO and then also having a bit of time to yourself - Be mindful of your own needs, but remember that this experience also only lasts a couple of months, so make sure to make the most of it. 
2. Vancouver is very expensive - Make sure to have plenty of savings, apply for scholarships/grants or borrow money. It is so annoying to miss out on experiences just because your bank account says no
3. UBC is VERY pedagogic - Don't get offended if they treat you a bit like you're a child, they mean well. Remember that their students are typically a lot younger and en in general more inexperienced than Danish university students, so that is why they really try to take care of their students

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: UBC has exchange students from all over the world, which is amazing. Remember to be respectful of other people's cultures, traditions, and so on - You may have heard a lot about other people's countries, and think that you know a lot, but you probably don't. Be curious - I found it extraordinary how my views of different countries have expanded and become more nuanced after having met so many different people.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding parts of the experience have been getting the chance to live in another country as great and beautiful as Canada and to feel all the personal growth that I have gone through. It would be too cliche to say that I have come home as a new person, but I see the world and myself differently now. I have definitely learned that my fate is probably not to stay in Denmark.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I will say that the greatest challenge was 100 % COVID's influence on the exchange - It made the move to another country very difficult and added a lot of insecurities during the planning. I actually moved my exchange from the autumn to the spring semester because of COVID, and I was honestly not sure that the exchange would be possible until my first day at UBC.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Exchange is the greatest experience of my life, and I recommend everyone to go no matter where you're interested in going - But you should 100 % consider going to Canada, and specifically UBC. It was everything I ever dreamed of and more. Go go go.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
